# Pseudospectrum of Non-Selfadjoint Elliptic Quadratic Differential Operators

This study focuses on the pseudospectrum of non-selfadjoint elliptic quadratic differential operators. These operators arise naturally through the Weyl quantization of complex-valued elliptic quadratic symbols, providing a rich framework in which the interplay between spectral theory and microlocal analysis can be examined. The non-selfadjoint character of these operators is central to the analysis, as it gives rise to phenomena that have no counterpart in the selfadjoint setting.

A principal contribution of this work is the establishment of a simple necessary and sufficient condition, formulated directly in terms of the Weyl symbol, that guarantees the stability of the spectra of these operators. This criterion offers a clear and verifiable means of determining whether an operator's spectrum is robust under perturbation, thereby distinguishing between well-behaved cases and those prone to instability.

When this stability condition is violated, the situation changes dramatically. In such cases, strong spectral instabilities emerge for the high energies of these operators. Remarkably, these instabilities may manifest in regions of the complex plane that lie far from the actual spectra of the operators. This means that even small perturbations can induce spectral behavior that is drastically different from what the unperturbed spectrum would suggest, underscoring the delicate nature of non-selfadjoint operators.

To make these phenomena precise, the paper provides a detailed geometrical description of the instability regions that arise under small perturbations. This analysis characterizes exactly where in the complex plane the spectral instabilities are located, offering a rigorous account of the structure and extent of these regions. The geometrical perspective thus transforms an abstract notion of instability into a concrete and quantifiable description.

Finally, this geometrical analysis has important practical implications. In particular, it explains why numerical algorithms designed for eigenvalue computation frequently produce false eigenvalues—spurious values located far from the true spectra of the operators. By identifying the regions in which such artifacts are expected to appear, the results shed light on a well-known difficulty in the numerical study of non-selfadjoint operators and provide theoretical grounding for the interpretation of computational results.

# Pseudospectra of Elliptic Quadratic Differential Operators

## Introduction and Motivation

The study of non-selfadjoint operators has revealed a fundamental phenomenon that distinguishes them sharply from their selfadjoint counterparts: the spectrum alone often fails to capture the true behavior of the operator under perturbation. Whereas the spectrum of a selfadjoint operator is stable in the sense that small perturbations produce only small displacements of eigenvalues, non-selfadjoint operators can exhibit dramatic spectral instabilities. Even minute perturbations may generate eigenvalues located far from the spectrum of the unperturbed operator. This sensitivity is precisely quantified by the notion of the *pseudospectrum*, which describes the regions of the complex plane where the resolvent norm becomes very large, or equivalently, where the operator is close—in an appropriate sense—to being non-invertible.

In this work, we investigate the pseudospectrum of a distinguished and analytically rich class of non-selfadjoint operators: the elliptic quadratic differential operators. These are operators defined through the Weyl quantization procedure applied to complex-valued quadratic symbols on phase space that satisfy an ellipticity condition. Because their symbols are quadratic, these operators enjoy a highly explicit structure—governed by the fundamental matrix associated with the quadratic form and by symplectic geometry—which makes them ideal objects for a precise microlocal analysis. At the same time, they arise naturally throughout mathematical physics and partial differential equations, for instance as models in kinetic theory, in the study of the Fokker–Planck and Kramers equations, and in the semiclassical analysis of resonances, so that understanding their spectral robustness is of both intrinsic and applied importance.

## Aims of the Analysis

Our central goal is to develop a detailed microlocal understanding of the spectral stability and instability phenomena that appear when these operators are subjected to small perturbations. The microlocal viewpoint is essential here: the mechanisms responsible for instability are localized in phase space, and their geometry is controlled by the interplay between the real and imaginary parts of the Weyl symbol along the flow it generates. By analyzing how energy propagates and concentrates under this dynamics, one can predict exactly where and how strongly the operator resists or succumbs to perturbation.

## Main Results

The core of our results is a dichotomy governed by a single, remarkably simple criterion imposed on the Weyl symbol.

**A necessary and sufficient condition for stability.** We first establish a clean necessary and sufficient condition on the quadratic Weyl symbol that guarantees spectral stability. When this condition holds, the pseudospectrum behaves benignly: the resolvent remains controlled outside a neighborhood of the spectrum, and the eigenvalues faithfully reflect the operator's response to small perturbations. In this regime, there is no hidden reservoir of pseudospectral behavior that could mislead one about the operator's true spectral properties.

**Strong instability when the condition fails.** When the stability condition is violated, the situation changes profoundly. We prove the existence of strong spectral instabilities occurring at high energies, in regions of the complex plane lying far from the actual spectrum of the operator. In these regions the resolvent norm grows extremely rapidly, so that the operator is exponentially close to singular even though the corresponding complex values are nowhere near genuine eigenvalues. We do more than establish the existence of this phenomenon: we provide a precise geometric characterization of the regions where these instabilities arise, describing them explicitly in terms of the symplectic and dynamical structure encoded in the Weyl symbol. This geometric description pinpoints the location, extent, and mechanism of the pseudospectral growth.

## Consequences for Numerical Computation

Beyond their intrinsic interest, these results have a direct and practical interpretation. Numerical eigenvalue algorithms, when applied to non-selfadjoint operators of this type, are known to produce spurious or "false" eigenvalues—computed values that appear to be part of the spectrum but do not correspond to any true eigenvalue. Our analysis explains this phenomenon rigorously: the false eigenvalues are precisely the manifestation of the strong pseudospectral instabilities we identify. Because the resolvent is enormous in the regions we characterize, finite-precision computation inevitably perceives the operator as singular there, generating artifacts far from the genuine spectrum. Thus the microlocal geometry of the pseudospectrum furnishes a complete and quantitative account of the spurious spectral behavior observed in numerical practice.

# The Weyl Legacy: Symmetry, Geometry, and the Structure of Nature

Few names resonate across both mathematics and physics as profoundly as that of Hermann Weyl. Our understanding of modern theoretical science owes a remarkable debt to his work, which bridged pure geometry, group theory, and the emerging frameworks of quantum mechanics and relativity.

## The Man Behind the Name

Hermann Weyl (1885–1955) was a German mathematician whose intellectual reach was extraordinarily broad. A student of David Hilbert, he moved fluidly between disciplines that others treated as separate territories. Our modern appreciation of symmetry as a foundational principle in physics traces much of its lineage to Weyl's insistence that the deep structure of nature could be captured through the language of groups and invariants.

## The Concept of Gauge Symmetry

Perhaps the most enduring contribution attributed to Weyl is his early formulation of gauge theory. In attempting to unify gravity and electromagnetism, he introduced the idea that physical laws should remain unchanged under certain local transformations. Although his original proposal did not succeed in its intended form, the underlying concept—gauge invariance—became one of the central pillars of contemporary particle physics. Our Standard Model of fundamental interactions is, at its heart, a gauge theory.

## The Weyl Fermion

In quantum field theory, the term "Weyl fermion" describes a massless particle governed by a simplified version of the Dirac equation. For decades these entities remained purely theoretical. Yet in recent years, condensed matter physicists have discovered materials known as Weyl semimetals, whose electronic behavior mimics these exotic particles. The Weyl fermion thus lives a curious double life: an abstraction from the 1920s that reappears as a measurable phenomenon in the laboratory.

## A Lasting Influence

The threads Weyl wove continue to shape research today. Whether through the mathematics of Lie groups, the philosophy of symmetry, or the physics of novel quantum materials, his ideas remain vibrant. Our continued exploration of these themes demonstrates how a single visionary thinker can leave an imprint that endures across generations of scientific inquiry.

## Abstract

We study the spectral instability of elliptic quadratic differential operators, a class of non-self-adjoint operators whose Weyl symbols are complex-valued quadratic forms with positive definite real part. While the spectra of such operators are discrete and can be computed explicitly in terms of the eigenvalues of the associated Hamilton map, the strong non-normality induced by the non-self-adjointness renders the spectrum highly unstable under small perturbations. To quantify this phenomenon, we investigate the $\varepsilon$-pseudospectrum, which captures the regions of the complex plane where the resolvent norm becomes anomalously large despite lying far from the spectrum itself.

Our main results provide a precise geometric characterization of the pseudospectra in terms of the numerical range and the Poisson bracket condition of Hörmander, Dencker, Sjöstrand, and Zworski. We show that for spectral values lying in the interior of the numerical range, the resolvent grows faster than any inverse power of the distance to the spectrum, and we establish exponential lower bounds $\|(P-z)^{-1}\| \geq C e^{c/h}$ in the semiclassical regime, demonstrating that the eigenvalues are exponentially sensitive to perturbations. These bounds are obtained through the explicit construction of quasimodes concentrated along the bicharacteristic flow, together with sharp resolvent estimates near the boundary of the numerical range.

We further analyze the transition behavior at the boundary of the numerical range, where subelliptic estimates yield resolvent bounds of intermediate order $\|(P-z)^{-1}\| \lesssim h^{-k/(k+1)}$ governed by the finite type of the symbol. As an application, we discuss consequences for the return-to-equilibrium problem for degenerate hypoelliptic operators of Kramers–Fokker–Planck type and illustrate the results with explicit computations for the non-self-adjoint harmonic oscillator and rotated Schrödinger operators. Our findings underscore that the classical spectrum provides an incomplete picture of the dynamics generated by these operators, and that the pseudospectrum offers the appropriate framework for understanding their genuine spectral behavior.

# Abstract

**Spectral Stability, False Eigenvalues, and Pseudospectral Analysis of Non-Self-Adjoint Quadratic Differential Operators**

We investigate the spectral properties of a class of quadratic differential operators of the form $\mathcal{L} = -\partial_x^2 + V(x)$, where the potential $V(x) = \alpha x^2 + i\beta x$ with $\alpha \in \mathbb{C}$, $\Re(\alpha) > 0$, and $\beta \in \mathbb{R}$, arising as models in the study of non-Hermitian quantum mechanics and hydrodynamic stability. Although such operators possess discrete spectra with eigenvalues admitting explicit representation, we demonstrate that their strong non-normality renders the eigenvalue expansions spectrally unstable under arbitrarily small perturbations.

Our principal contributions are threefold. First, we establish sharp resolvent norm estimates and characterize the $\varepsilon$-pseudospectra $\sigma_\varepsilon(\mathcal{L})$, proving that they extend into parabolic regions of the complex plane far exceeding the convex hull of the true spectrum. We derive precise semiclassical bounds on $\|(\mathcal{L} - z)^{-1}\|$ that grow exponentially as $\Im(z)$ increases, quantifying the departure from self-adjoint behavior via the Davies–Kuijlaars scaling exponent.

Second, we identify and rigorously analyze the phenomenon of *false eigenvalues*: spurious spectral values that emerge in finite-dimensional Galerkin and spectral collocation discretizations. We show that these numerical artifacts populate curves within the pseudospectrum rather than approximating genuine eigenvalues, and we provide asymptotic laws governing their distribution as the discretization dimension $N \to \infty$. A key result establishes a threshold relation between machine precision $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{mach}}$ and the maximal reliable eigenvalue index.

Third, we formulate computable *spectral stability conditions* based on the geometry of the numerical range and the condition number of the eigenvector basis. We prove that the eigenfunction system, though complete, fails to form a Riesz basis, and we characterize the growth of the associated spectral projections $\|P_n\| \sim e^{cn}$ using techniques from the theory of complex WKB analysis and exponentially weighted Sobolev spaces.

These results clarify the delicate interplay between mathematical spectral theory and numerical realization for non-self-adjoint operators, with implications for the reliability of spectral computations in convection–diffusion problems, damped wave equations, and PT-symmetric quantum systems. We conclude with numerical experiments illustrating the coalescence of computed spectra onto pseudospectral boundaries and confirming our theoretical predictions.

**Keywords:** non-self-adjoint operators, pseudospectra, spectral instability, false eigenvalues, quadratic potentials, resolvent estimates, semiclassical analysis, PT-symmetry

**Spectral Stability of Non-Self-Adjoint Operators: A Weyl Symbol Criterion and the Origin of Spurious Eigenvalues**

We establish a necessary and sufficient condition on the Weyl symbol of a pseudodifferential operator that characterizes spectral stability under small perturbations, and we demonstrate how the failure of this condition accounts for the appearance of false eigenvalues in numerical discretizations. For a semiclassical operator $P = \mathrm{Op}_h^w(p)$ acting on $L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$, we prove that spectral stability at a point $z \notin \sigma(P)$—understood as the boundedness of the resolvent norm $\|(P - z)^{-1}\|$ uniformly as $h \to 0$—holds if and only if the principal symbol satisfies a non-degeneracy condition on the characteristic set $p^{-1}(z)$, equivalent to the vanishing of the associated Poisson bracket obstruction $\{\operatorname{Re}(p-z), \operatorname{Im}(p-z)\}$ having a definite sign along bicharacteristics. When the condition fails, we show that the operator admits quasimodes—approximate eigenfunctions concentrated microlocally on the characteristic manifold—whose existence renders the resolvent norm exponentially large in $1/h$. In particular, the boundary of the numerical pseudospectrum converges to the level set determined by the bracket obstruction rather than to the true spectrum.

We illustrate the theory with the complex Airy operator, the rotated harmonic oscillator, and advection–diffusion operators arising in fluid stability analysis, confirming that computed eigenvalues cluster along the predicted pseudospectral curves. These results provide a rigorous framework for distinguishing genuine spectral data from discretization artifacts in the numerical analysis of non-self-adjoint problems.

# Spectral Instability of Elliptic Quadratic Differential Operators under Small Perturbations at High Energy

**Abstract**

We investigate the spectral stability properties of non-self-adjoint elliptic quadratic differential operators subject to small perturbations, with particular attention to the high-energy regime. Elliptic quadratic differential operators, defined via Weyl quantization of complex-valued quadratic symbols whose real part is positive definite, possess discrete spectra generated by their Hamilton map eigenvalues. While their spectra are explicitly computable in the unperturbed case, we demonstrate that these operators exhibit pronounced spectral instability: arbitrarily small perturbations can induce large deviations of eigenvalues from the unperturbed spectrum as one moves deeper into the semiclassical or high-energy limit.

This instability is quantified through the growth of the resolvent norm in regions of the complex plane lying outside the spectrum, where the associated pseudospectrum extends substantially beyond the spectral set. We show that the pseudospectral abscissa grows without bound at high energies, reflecting the strong non-normality of the operators and the departure of their resolvent behavior from that predicted by spectral projections alone. The underlying mechanism is governed by the symplectic geometry of the Hamilton map and the failure of a bracket (Hörmander-type) condition on the boundary of the numerical range, which permits the construction of quasimodes concentrating at high frequencies.

Our analysis combines microlocal and semiclassical techniques—including the construction of WKB-type approximate solutions and estimates on non-self-adjoint resolvents—to establish quantitative lower bounds on the perturbation-induced spectral displacement. These results clarify the sensitivity of computed spectra to numerical and modeling errors, and highlight fundamental limitations on spectral approximation for this class of operators. The findings have implications for the analysis of return-to-equilibrium rates, hypoelliptic evolution equations, and the reliability of spectral methods applied to non-normal operators arising in kinetic theory and mathematical physics.

*Keywords:* non-self-adjoint operators, quadratic differential operators, pseudospectrum, spectral instability, semiclassical analysis, Hamilton map
